chapter: Lucky Millinder and Duke Ellington's band, 1948-52
title: Third trombone, a lead part, and the name Monsieur du Beurre
summary: Jackson, a famous low-note player, found a lead passage in his third part; Duke said he heard him on it, and in Paris in 1950 called him Monsieur du Beurre.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: We had an arrangement in the book that -- I always played third because, like all the bands I've been in, everyone wanted to hear me play low notes. I had made a name around New York for playing low notes, "Get Butter to play third trombone," you know, --

-- or fourth. And I did it on a tenor trombone before a bass trombone. And I can make a bottom, I can make a good bottom with the tenor trombone. , So he made an arrangement -- I'm playing third -- and all at once for four measures I'm up on the first part. I said, "Now, something is the matter here." At the time John Sanders was doing the copying and I said, "Edward, didn't you make a mistake on my part?" I said, "Now, these four measures, I'm playing lead," and I said, "I have been playing third all the
time." So he said, you know, "Monsieur du Beurre," he said, "in those formations I heard you playing that top part."
What did he call you? Monsieur who?

Duke, when we went to Europe in '50, my nickname was Butter. Don Redman gave me that nickname when I first joined McKinney Cotton Pickers. I was young and tender and they said I looked like butter, so that stuck. So, anyway, --
Yes, yes, I was round. My cheeks was round and smooth. In Cincinnati they called me "Baby Boy," before I got to Detroit and they called me "Butter."
He said he heard you playing that first part.

Yeah. So he called me Monsieur du Beurre. Now, when we went to Paris in 1950, and Butter being my nickname, he found out that butter in French was Beurre, see. So after that he called me Monsieur du Beurre, you know, like Mr. Butter.
And it stuck. A lot of guys, you know, that went to Europe with me, it stuck with them, you know.
